paragraphs.title: The Shulammite in the Dance and the Description of Her Beauty

easy.explanation: The call is directed to the Shulammite: “Return, return, O Shulamite.”
easy.q: To whom is the repeated call “Return, return” addressed?

easy.explanation: They ask her to return and be seen in the dance.
easy.q: What are the women inviting the Shulammite to do?

easy.explanation: These verses describe her beauty from her feet to her head.

medium.explanation: The description begins, “How beautiful are thy feet with shoes.”
medium.q: With what does the description of the Shulammite begin?

answers: She is being invited to come back and be seen
She is being warned to leave
She is hiding from the dancers
medium.explanation: The repetition emphasizes the desire for her to return to the dance.
medium.q: What does the repeated phrase “Return, return” suggest?

medium.explanation: The passage mentions towers, fishpools, Mount Carmel, and purple.
medium.q: Which group of images appears in the description?

answers: Her desire to leave the group
challenge.explanation: The invitation highlights how she stands out within the group.
challenge.q: What does the invitation to see the Shulammite in the dance emphasize?

answers: From her feet upward to her head
From her head downward to her feet
From the countryside toward the city
challenge.explanation: The description moves from her feet, through her body and face, to her head.
challenge.q: What is the general direction of the description of her beauty?

answers: A rich and exalted picture of her beauty
A description of her daily work
An account of a long journey
challenge.explanation: The many comparisons magnify and honor her beauty.
challenge.q: What effect is created by comparing her features with jewels, nature, and impressive structures?

short_answers.question: In one short phrase, what is the main subject of verses 1–6?
short_answers.explanation: The verses focus on her being called to the dance and on the detailed description of her beauty.

paragraphs.title: The Lover’s Admiration and the Couple’s Intimacy

easy.explanation: He says, “How fair and how pleasant art thou, O love.”
easy.q: How does the lover describe the woman in verse 6?

easy.explanation: He says, “This thy stature is like to a palm tree.”
easy.q: To what does he compare her stature?

easy.explanation: The verses use images of grapes, apples, wine, fragrance, and lips.

answers: The beauty and loveliness of the beloved
The woman’s wish to leave the city
medium.explanation: Her breasts are compared with clusters of grapes as part of the lover’s praise.
medium.q: What does the image of clusters of grapes communicate?

answers: They express admiration and a desire for closeness
They show that the lovers are separated
They describe ordinary village life only
medium.explanation: Wine and fragrance convey sweetness, attraction, and intimacy.
medium.q: How do the images of wine and fragrance support the main idea?

answers: The upper part or palate of the mouth
medium.explanation: Here “roof” refers to the palate, or upper part, of the mouth.
medium.q: What does the KJV word “roof” mean in “the roof of thy mouth”?

answers: From admiration of beauty to expressions of intimacy
From vineyards to the city gates
challenge.explanation: The passage begins with praise and moves toward images of closeness and affection.
challenge.q: What is the main movement in verses 7–10?

answers: The beauty and graceful form of the beloved
Her connection with a particular city
challenge.explanation: The palm tree is used as a graceful image for her stature.
challenge.q: What does the comparison “thy stature is like to a palm tree” emphasize?

answers: It uses the images of wine and lips to express sweetness and closeness
It changes completely to language of distance
challenge.explanation: The sweet wine and speaking lips continue the passage’s intimate imagery.
challenge.q: How does verse 9 continue the language of admiration?

short_answers.question: In a short phrase, what do the images of wine and fragrance express?
answers: Admiration, sweetness, and desire for closeness
short_answers.explanation: These images express the sweetness of love and the desire for intimate fellowship.

paragraphs.title: The Beloved’s Invitation to the Vineyards and Fulfilled Love

answers: The beloved woman invites her lover
easy.explanation: She says, “Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field.”
easy.q: Who invites whom to go into the field?

answers: To the palace and city gate
easy.explanation: She proposes going into the field, lodging in the villages, and visiting the vineyards.
easy.q: Where does she suggest that they go?

easy.explanation: The passage mentions the flourishing vine, budding pomegranates, and fragrant mandrakes.
easy.q: Which plants or fruits are mentioned near the end of the passage?

answers: Going early to the vineyards to inspect them
medium.explanation: She says, “Let us get up early to the vineyards” and see whether the plants are flourishing.
medium.q: What does the beloved woman propose doing early in the morning?

answers: A young or newly developing grape
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to the young grape appearing on the vine.
medium.q: What does “the tender grape” refer to in the passage?

answers: Fresh produce and stored produce are both available
Only past events are being described
medium.explanation: She has pleasant fruits of both kinds laid up for her beloved.
medium.q: What is meant by “new and old” fruits?

answers: They create a setting of renewal prepared for a meeting
They show that the beloved wants to withdraw
They describe the end of the fruit season
challenge.explanation: Blossoming vines, young grapes, and budding pomegranates create a setting of renewal and readiness.
challenge.q: How do the spring images support the invitation?

answers: Go into the field, lodge in the villages, and rise early to visit the vineyards
Rise early in the vineyards, return to the city, and then enter the field
Stay in the city, prepare a feast, and leave at night
challenge.explanation: Her invitation follows the order of going out, lodging in the villages, and rising early to inspect the vineyards.
challenge.q: What sequence does the beloved woman suggest?

answers: The ripening of nature parallels love becoming ready for fulfillment
Nature prevents the lovers from meeting
The natural images have no connection with love
challenge.explanation: The passage connects the renewal and readiness of nature with the fulfillment of love.
challenge.q: What is suggested by joining the flourishing of nature with “there will I give thee my loves”?

short_answers.question: In one short phrase, what is the main setting of verses 11–14?
answers: A spring countryside of fields and vineyards
A royal palace in the city
short_answers.explanation: The beloved invites her lover into the field and vineyards, where spring growth is appearing.
